stages.name: Horizontal and conglomerate integration
stages.title: Horizontal and conglomerate integration
stages.sub: Recognise the two types of merger and explain three advantages of merging with a direct rival.

steps.q: A bakery merges with another bakery that makes the same kind of bread for the same customers. What stage of production are both firms at?
steps.right: The same stage, selling similar products
steps.wrong: Different stages of the same supply chain
steps.hint: Are the two bakeries rivals selling to the same customers, or one supplying the other?

steps.q: A bakery instead merges with a company that makes furniture, in a totally unrelated market. What stage or market do the two firms share?
steps.right: None, they are in unrelated markets
steps.wrong: The same market, just different products
steps.hint: Does furniture-making have anything to do with baking bread?

steps.q: After the two bakeries merge, they combine their ovens and delivery vans into one larger operation rather than running two separate small ones. What happens to their average cost per loaf?
steps.right: It falls, because output is spread over the bigger combined operation
steps.wrong: It rises, because two lots of equipment now need running
steps.hint: Think about economies of scale: does spreading fixed costs over more loaves raise or lower the cost per loaf?

steps.q: Before the merger, the two bakeries were competing for the same local customers. After merging into one firm, how many bakeries are now competing for those customers?
steps.right: Just one, so competition for those customers falls
steps.wrong: Still two, just under one owner

steps.q: One bakery had a much better bread recipe and the other had a much faster delivery app. After merging, can the combined firm use both together?
steps.right: Yes, both firms' strengths become available to the whole business
steps.wrong: No, each part can only use its own original strengths
